questions.text: A premature infant is delivered apneic with a heart rate of 80 beats/min. What is the most appropriate first action?

answers.text: Begin bag-mask ventilation at 40–60/min with room air
Begin chest compressions immediately
Apply 100% oxygen by nasal cannula and observe
Intubate and administer surfactant before any ventilation

questions.text: During resuscitation of a 32-week premature infant, what starting FiO₂ is recommended?

answers.text: 30% — for infants less than 35 weeks gestation
21% — room air is required for all premature infants
60% — premature lungs need a high baseline FiO₂
100% — to rapidly correct any shunt

questions.text: PPV has been provided for an apneic newborn, but the heart rate remains below 60/min. According to the resuscitation sequence, what should be done?

answers.text: Continue PPV first for 30 seconds; if there is no recovery, begin chest compressions
Begin chest compressions immediately and stop PPV
Increase FiO₂ to 100% and continue to observe
Stop resuscitation, as a heart rate below 60 is not survivable

questions.text: A newborn has an APGAR score of 5 at one minute of life. How is this interpreted?

answers.text: Below normal — a score less than 6 at 1 minute may require more aggressive support
Normal — any score of 5 or higher requires no intervention
A measure of gestational age rather than clinical status
An indication to immediately discontinue all support

questions.text: An infant weighs 1,200 grams at birth. How is this infant classified by weight?

answers.text: Very low birth weight (VLBW) — less than 1500 g
Low birth weight (LBW) — less than 2500 g but more than 1500 g
Extremely low birth weight (ELBW) — less than 1000 g
Normal birth weight

questions.text: On exam, a neonate has bounding peripheral pulses with a strong brachial pulse and a weak femoral pulse. What does this combination most suggest?

answers.text: A patent ductus arteriosus (with major left-to-right shunting), or possibly coarctation of the aorta
Hypovolemic shock with peripheral vasoconstriction
A normal newborn pulse pattern requiring no concern
Severe RDS from surfactant deficiency

questions.text: A grunting, flaring infant has a chest x-ray showing diffuse hazy reticulogranular (ground glass) densities with air bronchograms and low lung volumes. What is the most likely diagnosis and cause?

answers.text: Respiratory distress syndrome due to insufficient surfactant
Transient tachypnea of the newborn due to retained lung fluid
Meconium aspiration syndrome due to airway obstruction
Pulmonary interstitial emphysema due to barotrauma

questions.text: A term infant with RDS appears pink despite an ABG showing a PaO₂ of 30 mmHg. What best explains the absence of cyanosis?

answers.text: High fetal hemoglobin and hyperbilirubinemia can mask cyanosis even with severe hypoxemia
A PaO₂ of 30 mmHg is normal for a newborn
Cyanosis only appears when PaCO₂ is also elevated
Surfactant administration always restores normal color

questions.text: Why is surfactant ineffective at lowering alveolar surface tension in an infant born at 30 weeks, even though surfactant production began at 24 weeks?

answers.text: Before 34–35 weeks the surfactant is trapped inside the alveolar type II cells and cannot be released
Surfactant is not produced at all until 36 weeks of gestation
Fetal hemoglobin destroys surfactant before it reaches the alveoli
The ductus arteriosus prevents surfactant from reaching the lungs

questions.text: Pre- and post-ductal saturation probes show a difference of more than 5% between the right arm and the left lower leg. What does this indicate?

answers.text: A right-to-left shunt, most likely a patent ductus arteriosus and patent foramen ovale
A normal variation in newborn saturation readings
Inaccurate probes that should be repositioned
A left-to-right shunt that requires no further evaluation

questions.text: An infant has chronically elevated PCO₂ with normal oxygenation values. What is the best method to monitor the PCO₂ status?

answers.text: A capillary stick from the heel — accurate for PCO₂ and electrolytes
A capillary stick from the heel, relying on its oxygen value
Pulse oximetry alone, which reflects PCO₂
A pre-ductal saturation probe on the right hand
